# Incident Report — 2024-09-04 Traffic Analysis Exercise

## Victim Host
| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **172.17.0.99** |
| MAC address | **18:3d:a2:b6:8d:c4** |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-RNVO9AT** (domain: `bepositive.com`, workgroup name `BEPOSITIVE` also seen via NBNS) |
| Logged-in user | **afletcher** (confirmed via Kerberos `CNameString` on both the client and the domain controller exchange) |

Domain controller for context (not infected): 172.17.0.17, MAC 00:23:ae:50:ba:fd, hostname WIN-CTL9XBQ9Y19.

## Malware Family
**Koi Stealer** (Win32/Koi Stealer). **Attribution: signature-confirmed** — the supplied Suricata/IDS export contains a direct hit:

```
ETPRO TROJAN Win32/Koi Stealer CnC Checkin (POST) M2
172.17.0.99 -> 79.124.78.197
```

This is corroborated behaviorally in the pcap: 172.17.0.99 makes 96 repeated `POST /foots.php` requests to the bare IP `79.124.78.197` over port 80, each with `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`, `Content-Length: 40`, an MSIE 7.0-spoofed User-Agent, and an identical fixed-format body (`102|<GUID>`), running from 17:35 to 18:31 UTC — a classic fixed-interval C2 beacon with no DNS lookup for the destination (bare-IP host header), which is the strong C2 tell the IDS also flagged.

## Indicators of Compromise

**Command-and-control endpoint**
- `79.124.78.197:80` (TCP/HTTP) — primary C2 server, no associated domain (contacted directly by IP)

**C2 URIs observed**
- `GET http://79.124.78.197/index.php?id=&subid=qIOuKk7U` (single check-in/registration request)
- `POST http://79.124.78.197/index.php`
- `POST http://79.124.78.197/foots.php` — beacon loop, 96 occurrences, all returning HTTP 200 with empty body

**Beacon payload (grounded in traffic, from `/foots.php` POST bodies)**
- Fixed-format string: `102|30168213-3be0-a751-81a0-cf3b228c8654` (module code `102` + bot/session GUID `30168213-3be0-a751-81a0-cf3b228c8654`), sent unencrypted on every beacon
- `/index.php` registration response body observed: `HckDcK0czXjaq48jVHNn|qIOuKk7U|http://79.124.78.197/index.php|`

**User-Agent used by the malware**
- `Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 7.0; Windows NT 10.0; WOW64; Trident/7.0; .NET4.0C; .NET4.0E; .NET CLR 2.0.50727; .NET CLR 3.0.30729; .NET CLR 3.5.30729)` — spoofed/legacy IE UA, does not match a real Windows 10/11 browser, consistent with malware traffic

**Transferred files / hashes**
- No malware binary, dropper, or executable payload was transferred over any protocol visible in this capture (HTTP, SMB, TLS). The initial infection/delivery vector (e.g. the dropper download) occurred outside the window captured in this pcap. No SHA256 can be grounded from this evidence — none should be reported.

## Notes on other traffic (ruled out / benign context)
- `46.254.34.201` (TLS SNI `www.bellantonicioccolato.it`) — large byte transfer but is a normal HTTPS session to a legitimate-looking Italian business domain, not referenced in the IDS alerts; treated as benign/unrelated browsing, not a C2 indicator.
- SMB/NetBIOS alerts (`GPL NETBIOS SMB Session Setup NTMLSSP...overflow`, `SMB_COM_TRANSACTION Max Data Count of 0 DOS Attempt`, Kerberos principal overflow) between 172.17.0.99 and the domain controller 172.17.0.17 are standard AD authentication/SMB negotiation traffic that trips generic legacy Suricata overflow signatures; no evidence of exploitation or lateral movement was found in the corresponding packet payloads.
- All other TLS/DNS activity (Microsoft telemetry, Windows Update, MSN, Office, Bing, `msftconnecttest.com`, `login.microsoftonline.com`, Adobe ARM check) is standard Windows/enterprise background noise and not part of the compromise.

## Summary
DESKTOP-RNVO9AT (172.17.0.99, MAC 18:3d:a2:b6:8d:c4), logged in as domain user **afletcher** on the `bepositive.com` LAN, is infected with **Win32/Koi Stealer**, signature-confirmed by an ETPRO Suricata rule. The malware beacons every ~30–60 seconds to C2 **79.124.78.197:80** via `POST /foots.php`, sending a fixed bot-ID string, after an initial `GET/POST /index.php` registration. No dropper/payload file or hash is present in this capture; only the post-infection C2 phase is visible.
